newsitem.title: TANZANIA: IMF approves $235 million credit for Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: IMF approves $235 million credit for Tanzania.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund has approved $235 million in financial aid to Tanzania, restoring credit cut off in 1992, an IMF official said on Sunday.
The IMF suspended credits to Tanzania following allegations of corruption, including a huge import tax fraud.
"The approval was given last Friday by the executive board for the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility programme to Tanzania," IMF senior representative Festus Osunsade told Reuters.
"The commitment of ESAF loan resources represents an expression of confidence by the IMF in the economic and financial policy agenda of the Mkapa administration," he said.
The move followed sustained improvement in Tanzania's economic and financial indicators since January 1996, he said.
Improvements included reduced inflation and a slowdown in expansion of domestic money supply in relation to availability of goods and services.
Osunsade said the IMF loan, for which the first instalment of $40 million would be given next week, would help unlock extra financial assistance and external debt relief.
The IMF would be closely monitoring Tanzania's compliance with provisions of the agreement, he said, and it would be phased in line with continuing implementation of reforms.
Particular scrutiny would be given to the government's spending programme to ensure budget estimates were adhered to.

The government's medium-term goals include six percent annual growth by 1998/99, five percent annual inflation and an external current account deficit of 13.3 percent of GDP compared to a current 20.6 percent.
Annual inflation measured in September was 18.8 percent, trending down from a peak of over 43 percent in 1994.
"They've been put on a test. The IMF will be informing the international community of Tanzania's adherence to the conditions," said Osunsade.
Government officials were ecstatic.
"Tanzania's economic reform programme has always been dependent on foreign aid so we really welcome this decision," said one senior ministry of trade official.
"We have to get foreign capital into the economy and this could really help stimulate growth to the national budget."

One foreign banker said granting of the IMF credit was crucial for Tanzania's economic development following the start of liberalisation reforms 10 years ago. The socialist policies of founding president Julius Nyerere were scrapped in 1986.

"I think it is very necessary for Tanzania to have the support of the IMF. I believe the IMF is quite happy with Tanzania's performance because they have applied a very strict programme on Tanzania in order to get the loan," said Steven Forster, senior manager of South Africa's Stanbic bank based in Dar es Salaam.

The decision is likely to trigger a soft loan worth $100 million from the World Bank while the Paris Club of donors could agree to more than $220 million in debt relief, Osunsade said. Tanzania has a net foreign debt of about $7.8 billion.
President Benjamin Mkapa left on Sunday for official visits to Britain and Italy. He was expected to press Britain for debt relief and attend the World Food Summit in Rome.
One of the world's poorest countries, Tanzania enjoys a reputation as a stable, peaceful democracy with vast under-exploited potential in minerals, agriculture and tourism.
($1=600 Tanzanian shillings)
